strings.path.title: Sweep Picking
strings.path.goal: Sweep clean, separated arpeggios from three-string triads to six-string shapes, and link them through minor-key progressions so they sound like a solo.
strings.path.assumes: You can alternate-pick single notes evenly at sixteenths around 80 BPM (Alternate Picking through its Intermediate Level covers this) and you can hammer on and pull off cleanly. You don't need any sweeping yet, and you can start at whichever Level suits you.
strings.path.gradingLimits: Grading stops being trustworthy at about 150 ms between notes: sixteenths at 100 BPM, eighth triplets at 133, sextuplets at 66. Rungs faster than that are self-checked, whatever they look like, and the card says where grading stops. That line is a cautious policy, not a measurement. What a sweep is graded on is timing: how even the notes are, whether each one arrived, and whether extra notes crept in. Right notes are not graded anywhere on this Path: swept notes ring into each other, and a pitch read on ringing strings can fail a take that was played right, so nothing here promises them. The tests behind these numbers used synthetic tones, and no real guitar has been through them yet. The note after a slide counts as missed if it isn't heard, so bars on sliding shapes are lower; a tap counts as a note that must be heard, and a hammer or pull that isn't heard costs nothing. In practice: Beginner is graded at every rung. In Intermediate the sixteenth-note shapes stop at 100 BPM, triplet shapes at 130, and the sextuplet pickup at 65. In Advanced most of what makes the playing hard can't be graded. Sound never tells us the two things that matter most here, muting and pick path, and the Exercises say so.
strings.path.skills.0: Even alternate picking at sixteenths, 80 BPM
strings.step.triads.title: Three-string triads, up and down
strings.step.triads.goal: Sweep a minor and a major triad on the top three strings, up and back down, in even triplets, with each note separate.
strings.step.triads.why: This is the sweep everyone recognises: three notes of a chord in one push, A, C, E going up and E, C, A coming back. Three strings is the size every bigger shape is made of, and it's short enough to keep clean from the first day. Triplets put one sweep on every click, so the rhythm tells you where each stroke starts. You learn major and minor together because they differ by one note, and hearing that note is what turns a shape into a chord you can use.
strings.step.triads.howTo.0: One push per click. Going up the strings, the pick falls through the G, B and E strings in one downward motion and comes to rest on each string before it plays it. Coming back, the same in reverse: one upward pull through E, B and G. The last Exercise turns the pick at both ends with no repeated note, in sixteenths.
strings.step.triads.howTo.1: The top note is played twice, once at the end of the push and once at the start of the pull. That repeated note is the only place the pick changes direction.
strings.step.triads.howTo.2: Fretting hand: lift each finger's pressure as soon as the next note sounds, without leaving the string. Picking hand: the side of the palm rests lightly on the strings you have just left. Those two together are the mute.
strings.step.triads.howTo.3: The A minor shape at fret 12: little finger on the G string at 14, middle finger on the B string at 13, index on the top string at 12. For C major only the G string changes, to fret 12.
strings.step.triads.payoff: A minor and C major arpeggios that sound like chords being spelled out, and a four-chord progression played as sweeps, in your first session.
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.title: Two strings: the push and the pull
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.purpose: The smallest sweep there is: two notes of the triad in one push of the pick, a silent triplet to stop them, then the same two notes in one pull back. Everything a bigger sweep needs is here, the rest stroke and the mute, with nothing else to think about.
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.howTo.0: Triplets: two notes, then a silent third. Push down through both strings in one motion; the pick lands on the second string, rests there for a moment, then goes through it. Coming back, one pull up through both.
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.howTo.1: On the B and top strings in A minor: middle finger on the B string at 13, index on the top string at 12. Let go of the first note as the second sounds, without lifting the finger off the string.
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.howTo.2: Use the silent third to stop both strings. If you can hear them in the gap, the mute is what to work on, not the speed.
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.coachLin: Timing only: I time the notes and say if one went missing or rang on as an extra. Whether it was one push or two strokes is yours to keep honest.
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.detectio: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
strings.exercise.triads.two-string-push.selfChec: In each silent beat, were both strings quiet?
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.title: Triad rolls: two chords
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.purpose: Continuous triplet rolls on a pair of chords, a bar each: up the strings, back down, up, back. Each pair changes one or two notes, so you hear minor and major under your own fingers, and a different pair comes round on each Take.
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.howTo.0: Up, back, up, back in each bar: four sweeps, twelve notes, one sweep to a click. The top note is played twice, once at the end of the push and once at the start of the pull: that is where the pick turns.
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.howTo.1: Move only the fingers whose notes change at the bar line. Say the chord name as you arrive: if you hear the change before you name it, your ears are doing their job.
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.howTo.2: In the C to C minor pair the last beat is silent: stop the strings and bring the pick back above the G string without touching anything. Anything still ringing in that beat is a mute to fix.
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.coachLine: I grade timing and notes heard. Right notes aren't graded on a sweep, because the strings ring into each other, so name each chord yourself.
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.detection.0: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.selfCheck.0: Record a take and listen back. Does each note stop as the next one starts, or do they ring together like a strummed chord?
strings.exercise.triads.triad-rolls.selfCheck.1: In a silent beat, were all six strings quiet?
strings.exercise.triads.four-chords-rock.title: Am, F, C, G, rocking
strings.exercise.triads.four-chords-rock.purpose: A real four-chord progression played as sweeps, one bar per chord. Each shape is the one nearest the last, so the hand moves a fret or two at most, and it changes key from Take to Take.
strings.exercise.triads.four-chords-rock.howTo.0: Up, back, up, back on every chord. Move the fingers during the last note of the bar, and arrive on the first note of the next shape on the click.
strings.exercise.triads.four-chords-rock.howTo.1: Before you start, play the four chords once as ordinary strums so your ear knows where the music is going.
strings.exercise.triads.four-chords-rock.coachLi: A chord change is where notes go missing. If one does, I'll count it, and the bar line is where to look.

strings.exercise.triads.picked-turn.title: A turn with no hammer
strings.exercise.triads.picked-turn.purpose: Four notes with both ends turned by the pick alone, because you won't always have a hammer. It is the hard version: the pick really does change direction, twice.
strings.exercise.triads.picked-turn.howTo.0: Sixteenths. Stay small. After the bottom note, the next note is a downstroke, and after the top note, the next is an upstroke. Feel them as one elastic motion.
strings.exercise.triads.picked-turn.coachLine: This one gets fast quickly, and above the graded rungs it is yours to judge.

strings.step.turnaround.title: The turn at the top: hammer and pull-off
strings.step.turnaround.goal: Turn the sweep round at the top with a hammer and a pull, so it loops with no repeated note and no extra pick stroke.
strings.step.turnaround.why: In the last Step the pick turned round on a repeated note, or by itself. Real sweep lines don't repeat the top note: they add one more chord tone on the top string with a hammer, pull back off it, and sweep down. The hammer and the pull give the pick a moment with nothing to do, which is exactly when it changes direction, so the turn can't be heard. This loop is the sound of a sweep in a solo, and three strings is the cheapest place to learn it.
strings.step.turnaround.howTo.0: After the top string's push, the next note is a hammer-on, so the pick has nothing to do. Use that moment to turn it round.
strings.step.turnaround.howTo.1: The pull-off back is the last note before the upward push begins. Keep the pull clean: pull slightly sideways, off the string, and do not just lift.
strings.step.turnaround.howTo.2: Start with C major: its reach on the top string is three frets. The minor shapes reach five, and they come next.
strings.step.turnaround.payoff: A triad that loops without a seam, with the turn inaudible, at a tempo you can sing along with.
strings.exercise.turnaround.major-loop.title: C major, the short reach
strings.exercise.turnaround.major-loop.purpose: The whole loop with the shortest top-string reach. G, C, E, then hammer to G and back.
strings.exercise.turnaround.major-loop.howTo.0: Triplets. The first note of the loop after the first pass is an upstroke: the sweep comes back through it and turns, so you are never starting over.
strings.exercise.turnaround.major-loop.coachLine: I time each note and count the ones that arrived. A quiet hammer or pull costs nothing, so don't dig in to please me.
strings.exercise.turnaround.major-loop.detection: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.

strings.exercise.turnaround.minor-mid.title: Am at fret 8
strings.exercise.turnaround.minor-mid.purpose: A minor shape with a four-fret reach. The same loop, and your little finger starts earning its keep.
strings.exercise.turnaround.minor-mid.howTo.0: First finger on fret 8 of the top string, second on fret 9 of the G, third on fret 10 of the B, little finger hammering at fret 12. One finger per note: no rolling on this shape.
strings.exercise.turnaround.minor-mid.coachLine: Same bar as the last one. If it slips, the stretch is the place to look.

strings.exercise.turnaround.minor-high.howTo.0: First finger on fret 12, little finger on 17. If the reach is too much for now, slide up to it instead: the sound is what counts.

strings.step.phrases.title: Sweeps inside phrases
strings.step.phrases.goal: Use a sweep as part of a line that goes somewhere, starting and ending in a scale or on a held note.
strings.step.phrases.why: Nobody wants to hear ten bars of arpeggio. What makes a sweep sound exciting is what comes either side of it: a line that arrives by sweep, then sings; a run that shoots up to a held bend. This Step turns the shapes into something you could actually play in a solo.
strings.step.phrases.howTo.0: The held note after a sweep matters more than the sweep. Give it time and a little vibrato.
strings.step.phrases.howTo.1: Change technique cleanly. When a sweep ends, you go straight back to normal picking, with no moment of confusion in the hand.
strings.step.phrases.howTo.2: Use these as starting points. Write your own ending as soon as you can play the written one.
strings.step.phrases.payoff: Four phrases you can actually use in a solo, each one ending in a note that sings.

strings.exercise.phrases.sweep-then-scale.purpos: Up the Am shape, then run back down the scale with pull-offs. It is the most natural sweep phrase there is, and it ends on a held A with vibrato.
Hammer to 17, then three pull-offs on the top string (each pull sounds the next note), then pick the run down the B and G strings.

strings.exercise.phrases.triad-pair.howTo.0: Three up, pull off to fret 10, two more upstrokes down the strings. Loop it. It works over A minor or over a G chord, and hearing that is worth a minute.

strings.step.qualities.title: Triads up the neck
strings.step.qualities.goal: Play the same minor and major triad in three places up the neck, with the shifts landing on time.
strings.step.qualities.why: A shape you know in one place is a shape you can only use in one place. Every triad has three shapes on the top three strings, one per inversion, and between them they cover the neck, so whatever chord comes next, one of its shapes is under your hand. Learning them as loops that climb and come back is also your first real position-shift drill.
strings.step.qualities.howTo.0: Name the notes out loud as you practise, at least once. The spelled notes on each Exercise are there for that.
strings.step.qualities.howTo.1: Moving between inversions, shift during the last note of the bar, and arrive on the first finger of the new shape.
strings.step.qualities.payoff: A minor, C major and D minor in three places each, so the next chord always has a shape near your hand.
strings.exercise.qualities.minor-inversions.purp: The same three notes in three shapes up the neck, so you can reach for Am wherever your hand happens to be.
strings.exercise.qualities.minor-inversions.howT: Low shape is a one-finger barre roll at fret 5, the middle at fret 8 and the high at fret 12. Be ready on the new shape before the bar line.

strings.step.first-solo.title: Your first sweep solo, with the band
strings.step.first-solo.goal: Play looped three-string triads through two progressions over a band, and a four-bar sweep solo that ends on a held note.
strings.step.first-solo.why: Everything so far has been against a click. A band changes how it feels: the bass plays the roots, the drums carry the beat, and your arpeggios suddenly sound like a guitar solo instead of an exercise. Three strings is enough for that, and it's short enough that you can listen to the band while you play. The four-bar solo at the end is the Beginner Level's finish line.
strings.step.first-solo.howTo.0: Use direct input or headphones for a graded take. A microphone also hears the band, and that hasn't been tested.
strings.step.first-solo.howTo.1: Lock the first note of each bar to the kick drum and let the rest of the bar fall into place.
strings.step.first-solo.howTo.2: Turn the band down until your mistakes show. A loud band covers a ringing string.
strings.step.first-solo.payoff: You play a sweep solo over a band that follows the chords and ends on a note that sings.

strings.exercise.first-solo.band-three.howTo.0: Two loops a bar. The shapes are all near fret 12, and F slides to its top note because the reach is too wide to hammer.

strings.step.five-strings.goal: Own the two common five-string shapes with the root on the A string, in minor and major.
strings.step.five-strings.why: Five strings is the big sweep, the sound people mean when they say the word. strings.step.five-e-shape.title: Five strings: the E-shape, and a tap at the top
strings.step.five-e-shape.goal: Sweep the E-shape arpeggios that start on the fifth, and add a tapped note above the top of a five-string shape.
strings.step.five-e-shape.why: The A-shape puts the root on the A string. The E-shape is the barre chord you already know from the low E string, swept from the A string up, so it starts on the chord's fifth. Between the two shapes you have a minor and a major arpeggio in every part of the neck, often in the same place, which is what lets a progression stay under one hand. The tap is the other half of the classic sound: one more note above the shape, played by the picking hand, so the arpeggio reaches higher than the fretting hand can stretch.
strings.step.five-e-shape.howTo.0: E-shape: the first note is on the A string, then one note a string up to the top, and a hammer to the top note. There's no second note on the A string, so the bottom turn is a pick turn, and the rest after each loop gives you time for it and a moment to check the mute.
strings.step.five-e-shape.howTo.1: Tap with the middle finger of the picking hand, holding the pick tucked against the palm. Tap firmly on the fret, then pull off slightly downward so the fretted note under it sounds.
strings.step.five-e-shape.howTo.2: While you tap, the fretting hand keeps holding the note you pull off to. The tap is a loud attack and it counts as a note that must be heard.
strings.step.five-e-shape.payoff: Two five-string shapes per chord, and a tapped A minor sweep that reaches up to fret 20.

strings.step.the-link.title: The link: two shapes
strings.step.the-link.goal: Get from one arpeggio into the next with no gap and no extra pick stroke, slowly enough to hear the join.
strings.step.the-link.why: Linked arpeggios are what make a sweep sound like a solo and not an exercise, and the link is a separate skill from either shape. Almost everyone practises the shapes and hopes the join comes along. It doesn't: the join is where the pick stops, the hand arrives late and a note gets lost. So here it gets practised alone, as slowly as you like, with nothing else to think about.
strings.step.the-link.howTo.0: A link is one small move of the fretting hand. On the top or bottom string, step from the last note of the old shape to the nearest note of the new one with a hammer, a pull or a slide. The pick does nothing at that moment.
strings.step.the-link.howTo.1: Choose the nearest note of the new chord, not the root. Good links barely move the hand, which is why the shapes here may look unfamiliar.
strings.step.the-link.howTo.2: Look ahead. Know the note you are stepping to before you play the note you are stepping from.
strings.step.the-link.howTo.3: Keep muting through the change: the last note of the old shape stops as the new one sounds.
strings.step.the-link.payoff: You hear one line carry on across a chord change, and a chord change that happens under your fingers instead of between two shapes.

strings.exercise.the-link.link-alone.howTo.0: Bar 1 is the end of the old shape, bar 2 the start of the new one. The first note of bar 2 is not picked: hammer, pull or slide to it, and only then cross to the next string.
strings.exercise.the-link.link-alone.howTo.1: Say the chord names. If you can't tell which chord you're on, slow down until you can.
strings.exercise.the-link.link-alone.coachLine: Very slow on purpose. Say each chord's name as you land on it: that's the check that matters here.

strings.exercise.the-link.two-shapes.howTo.0: Triplets that take a whole bar for three notes. The pick pushes up through three strings, waits, then pushes down through the next shape.

strings.step.link-chains.title: Chains of links
strings.step.link-chains.goal: Link four chords in a row on three strings, without stopping, in any minor key.
strings.step.link-chains.why: Once two shapes link, the question becomes how long you can keep it going. A four-chord chain is the unit of real playing, and the minor-key loops here are the most common things you will be asked to sweep over. The moves are small, so the hard part is keeping your place: you should know which chord is next without counting.
strings.step.link-chains.howTo.0: Learn the chords by ear first. Play the progression's roots, once through, on the low strings.
strings.step.link-chains.howTo.1: Each chord's shape starts as near as it can to the last one. Don't reach for the shape you know best: reach for the nearest one.
strings.step.link-chains.howTo.2: If a link trips you, go back to two shapes and repeat that one link. Don't push through it.
strings.step.link-chains.payoff: A four-chord minor progression comes out of one unbroken sweep, in whichever key you land on today.

strings.step.long-chains.title: Four and five strings, linked
strings.step.long-chains.goal: Chain the big shapes, and mix short and long shapes in one line.
strings.step.long-chains.why: The bigger the shape, the further the hand has to come back at the end of it, so links on five strings need more planning than links on three. It also pays best: this is the sound of a fast minor-key lead break. Mixing lengths matters too, because a line of one length sounds like a pattern, and a three-string shape in the middle of big ones gives you somewhere to breathe.
strings.step.long-chains.howTo.0: Plan the link from the bottom of each shape: the last note on the A string walks to the first note of the next shape.
strings.step.long-chains.howTo.1: With five strings there's a lot to keep silent, and the mute has to travel across every change as well.
strings.step.long-chains.howTo.2: Mixed lengths: keep the beat the same when the shape gets shorter. The short shape fills the bar with two loops.
strings.step.long-chains.payoff: A long chain over a whole progression, big enough to sound like a solo.

strings.step.minor-progressions.title: Minor keys and the V chord
strings.step.minor-progressions.goal: Link through the harmonic-minor movement: the major V chord pulling back to i.
strings.step.minor-progressions.why: A natural-minor loop goes round forever and never needs to resolve. The major V chord is what changes that: its G# sits a half step under A and pulls back to it, and that pull is the dark, dramatic sound of metal and neoclassical playing. These progressions are shared vocabulary, and the thing to learn is the half-step move: it is the link you will come to love.
strings.step.minor-progressions.howTo.0: E major in A minor contains G#, a note A minor doesn't have. Find it in the shape. It is where the sound comes from.
strings.step.minor-progressions.howTo.1: Aim for the G# to A step at the resolution, and hear it before you play it.
strings.step.minor-progressions.howTo.2: Bdim to E to Am is the minor two-five-one. It is the same pull with one more chord of warning.
strings.step.minor-progressions.payoff: You hear a chord pull back to the minor at the end of a sweep, and a progression sounds like it's going somewhere.

strings.step.six-strings.title: Six strings
strings.step.six-strings.goal: Own a clean six-string sweep from the low E, minor and major, and link passes across all six.
strings.step.six-strings.why: Six strings is the longest push you can make, and it is a real physical challenge, since the arm travels the whole width of the neck and every string behind the pick has to stay quiet. It adds less new music than the step from three to five did. Come to it for the sound and for the discipline: a clean six-string sweep shows up any weakness in your muting at once.
strings.step.six-strings.howTo.0: The arm does this. The wrist stays quiet, and the forearm carries the pick from the low E to the high E in one long push.
strings.step.six-strings.howTo.1: Muting is the whole game: palm on what's behind the pick, the fretting fingers rolling off what's in front of it. Low strings ring loudest, so check them first.
strings.step.six-strings.howTo.2: Grading on these is limited: only the slowest rungs are graded, and even those have never been tried on a real guitar.
strings.step.six-strings.payoff: A sweep from the lowest note on the guitar to near the highest, with every note separate.

strings.step.six-string-changes.title: Six strings through the changes
strings.step.six-string-changes.goal: Change chord with the six-string shapes: a minor shape into its major, four chords in a minor key, and a six-string shape joined to a five-string and a three-string one.
strings.step.six-string-changes.why: The last Step gave you two six-string shapes, each looped on one chord, and single passes linked through a progression. Looping a whole shape on each chord of a progression is harder: a shape this wide is slow to leave, with six strings to quiet and a new place to find before the next bar. This Step adds no new shape. It takes the minor and the major shape through changes, slowly, so the move between them gets the practice the shapes have already had.
strings.step.six-string-changes.howTo.0: Each bar is one chord. In the sixteenth-note lines every bar ends with a rest: stop every string in it, then move the hand.
strings.step.six-string-changes.howTo.1: The pass tempos are slow on purpose. These shapes are wide, and the change has to be clean before it is fast.

strings.step.fast-shifts.title: Wide shapes and fast shifts
strings.step.fast-shifts.goal: Jump between shapes far apart on the neck, and play sweeps fast enough that grading no longer applies.
strings.step.fast-shifts.why: Everything until now has moved a fret or two. Sometimes a line needs an octave jump, and that's a throw of the whole arm that has to land exactly. This is also where speed comes in, so it's where the app can't help much: you'll be working by recording and by ear, as players always have.
strings.step.fast-shifts.howTo.0: Look at the landing spot before you leave. The hand follows the eye.
strings.step.fast-shifts.howTo.1: A shift is one fast movement and then stillness. Land early and let the note come to you.
strings.step.fast-shifts.howTo.2: Fast rungs are self-checked. Record yourself and slow the recording down: nothing is more honest than that.
strings.step.fast-shifts.payoff: A line that jumps the neck, and a burst of sweep at a speed you couldn't have played a month ago.

strings.step.neoclassical.title: Neoclassical sequences
strings.step.neoclassical.goal: Play the moves that give this style its sound: diminished shapes climbing in minor thirds, and triads walking up the harmonic minor scale.
strings.step.neoclassical.why: Baroque-flavoured metal comes from a few harmonic ideas played very fast: the major V, the diminished seventh on its leading tone, and triads walked in sequence. You've met the first two. A sequence adds the sense of a long line unfolding, and a diminished chord that moves three frets at a time is the most fun you can have with one shape.
strings.step.neoclassical.howTo.0: A diminished seventh is the same four notes every three frets. So G#dim7, Bdim7, Ddim7 and Fdim7 are one sound in four places.
strings.step.neoclassical.howTo.1: In a sequence, hear each bar as the next step of one melody. The top notes usually tell the tale.
strings.step.neoclassical.howTo.2: These are original lines in a shared style, and meant as starting points: write your own as soon as you can.
strings.step.neoclassical.payoff: The unmistakable sound of a neoclassical run, in lines you can change and call your own.

strings.step.advanced-etude.title: The Advanced etude
strings.step.advanced-etude.goal: Play an eight-bar piece in E minor that puts the Level's moves together: six-string shapes, a diminished shape climbing the neck, a shift between positions and the major five chord pulling home, in two halves and then with a band.
strings.step.advanced-etude.why: The Level has given you its moves one at a time: six strings, shifts, the diminished shape, the major five chord. A piece asks for them in a row with no time to set up, and that is a different skill from playing each one well. So it comes in halves: four bars until they hold, the next four, then the join, then the band.
strings.step.advanced-etude.howTo.0: The piece is eight bars of triplets in E minor: E minor, C, G and D# diminished 7, then E minor, A minor, B and E minor.
strings.step.advanced-etude.howTo.1: Parts one and two are against a click. Bring each to its pass tempo before joining them.
strings.step.advanced-etude.howTo.2: With the band, use direct input or headphones for a graded take: a microphone hears the band as well, and that has not been tested.
strings.step.advanced-etude.howTo.3: Grading is timing only: how even the notes are, whether each one arrived, and whether extra notes rang. Nothing here checks which notes you played or how clean the mute is, so record a take and listen.
strings.step.advanced-etude.payoff: An eight-bar sweep solo over a band, with six-string shapes, a diminished climb and a major five chord in it, played from start to finish.
